Issued at 215 PM CDT Wed Sep 23 2026

Light rain showers located along and south of Highway 20 will 
continue to drift east and taper off by early to mid afternoon 
today. Highs will be in the mid 60s west of I-29 and in the low 70s 
to the east where clouds have cleared.

Looking aloft we have a low amplitude ridge centered over the 
northern Plains. To the west over the north central Rockies a weak 
jet streak is lifting a shortwave east-northeast. To the southwest 
over the Four Corners region a second shortwave begins to slowly 
move northeast. These waves will be the driving force behind a few 
rounds of slow moving showers and thunderstorms. Looking aloft to 
the east we see a Rex block over southern Ontario and down into the 
Ohio Valley. This block is responsible for the slow progression of 
storms over the next 24-48 hours. Looking at the mid-levels moderate 
Theta-e advection brings north warmer and moist air that pools over 
central Nebraska, South Dakota, and North Dakota, ahead of the first 
wave. By mid-afternoon the LLJ begins to increase as the wave 
arrives with a strong push of WAA. From the southwest a band of 
positive vorticity advects in, further increasing dynamic forcing. A 
band of showers and thunderstorms are expected to form along this 
juncture in central South Dakota late this afternoon. Severe weather 
is not anticipated, however there exists enough shallow instability 
that a few stronger thunderstorms may produce brief periods of heavy 
rain. This north/south band of storms will slowly progress east 
through the evening and overnight. Around Sunrise Thursday storms 
should be along and west of I-29, and ending over central South 
Dakota. Storms continue to slowly progress east through Minnesota 
and Iowa the remainder of the day Thursday with showers ending from 
west to east through the late afternoon and evening. Highs for 
Thursday will once again be cooler than average for this time of 
year, in the low 60s east of Highway 81, and upper 60s to low 70s 
west. 

Through the course of the day Thursday, the Four Corners wave will 
move slowly northeast. By late Thursday evening into early Friday 
morning the Rex block that was slowing everything down will begin to 
break down. This will allow the wave to accelerate northeast through 
the overnight. With it will come a strong push of WAA and a strong 
band of vorticity advection. As dynamic forcing increases 
showers and thunderstorms will form along the leading edge of 
these elements. Storms move north and increase in areal coverage
through the day Friday, becoming widespread. Once again severe 
weather is not anticipated, but some lightning and brief heavy 
rain are possible. Meanwhile, a strong trough will push into the
Pacific Northwest through the day Friday. As it ejects out onto
the northern Plains overnight into Saturday it will begin to 
push the existing storms to the east. The strong upper trough 
will keep pushing everything out of the region and storms will 
taper off from west to east early Saturday afternoon through the
evening. 

As far as rainfall totals are concerned, the GFS, EC, and CAN 
ensembles have fluctuated a bit but over all keep the main band of 
higher accumulation from roughly northeast Nebraska into southwest 
Minnesota. HiRes guidance has some shifts west or east to the 
heaviest band but for the most part they align with the ensembles. 
LREF probabilities from now until 7pm Saturday indicate a greater 
than 80% probability for widespread 0.25 inches of rain. Increasing 
totals narrow in a similar pattern to the model guidance of highest 
precipitation, with a 40-80% probability of 1 inch of total rain. 
Please note, isolated pockets of 1+ inches are also possible.
Localized ponding is possible, as well as rises in creeks and
streams, but river flooding is not expected at this time. 

Saturday overnight will be dry and so will Sunday. By Sunday 
afternoon a few peaks of sunshine will be possible. Thanks to 
continuous southerly to southeasterly winds and WAA during this 
time, highs will gradually increase from Friday onward. Friday will 
see highs in the mid to upper 60s. Saturday and Sunday will see 
highs in the mid 60s to low 70s. Alas, our warmer and dry conditions 
will be short lived. Beginning Monday a series of waves brings more 
chances for rain and thunderstorms for the first half of the week. 
Highs will trend down from the mid 70s to the low 60s.
